script.opening: "Hello — I’m ringing about my bone scan. The lady said my bones are thin? I’ve been up half the night reading about it and I’m terrified — does this mean my bones are crumbling, that I’ll end up bent over or in a wheelchair? And I read about those bone tablets rotting your jaw, so I’ll be honest, I don’t want to take those. Is there anything natural instead? I just want to know how bad it is."

facts.text: T-score −2.7 at the hip = osteoporosis (≤−2.5). She has already had a FRAGILITY fracture (low-trauma wrist fracture from standing height) — which, with the DEXA and high FRAX, places her firmly in the treat category. Risk factors: early menopause (44), maternal hip fracture, ex-smoker.

HIDDEN AGENDA layer one — she has catastrophised "thin bones" into imminent disability (wheelchair, hunched, "crumbling"), fuelled by night-time googling. The anxiety is the presenting state; the result needs reframing accurately, neither minimised nor inflated.

HIDDEN AGENDA layer two — she’s read scare stories about bisphosphonates (osteonecrosis of the jaw, "poison") and is inclined to refuse; she half-wants permission to avoid them. The fear is real but the absolute risks are tiny versus the fracture-prevention benefit, which she hasn’t had explained.

If reached: her mother’s hip fracture led to a nursing home and death within a year; Patricia is privately terrified of "becoming my mother" and losing independence. This is the engine under both the catastrophising and the treatment ambivalence.

Officially: to know how bad it is and to avoid the "jaw-rotting" tablets. What is needed: accurate reframing (osteoporosis is treatable, not crumbling-to-a-wheelchair), honest balanced information on bisphosphonates (tiny absolute risks vs real fracture-prevention benefit), calcium/vitamin D + lifestyle, and her mother-fear addressed — supporting an informed decision.

ice.ideas: "Thin bones" means her skeleton is crumbling and she’ll end up disabled/in a wheelchair; the bone tablets rot your jaw and are "poison".
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — her mother’s hip fracture led to a care home and death within a year; she’s terrified of "becoming my mother" and losing independence; fear of bisphosphonate side-effects.
ice.expectations: To be told how bad it is and to be let off the "jaw-rotting" tablets. What she needs: accurate reframing, honest balanced bisphosphonate information, lifestyle/calcium-vitD, and her mother-fear addressed for an informed decision.

cues: "Crumbling / wheelchair / bent over" — catastrophised picture from googling; reframe accurately without dismissing.
"Tablets that rot your jaw / poison / something natural" — treatment fear and a wish for permission to refuse; give honest absolute risk.
A fragility wrist fracture + T-score −2.7 + maternal hip fracture — firmly in the treat group; this matters.

checkpoints.text: Interprets the result correctly and reframes it accurately: T-score ≤−2.5 = osteoporosis; explains it as reduced bone density and increased FRACTURE RISK — treatable and modifiable — NOT "crumbling" or inevitable disability/wheelchair

Recognises the FRAGILITY FRACTURE as decisive: a low-trauma wrist fracture plus osteoporotic DEXA and high FRAX places her clearly in the treat category (NICE NG259 10-year risk with FRAX or QFracture; NOGG 2024 intervention thresholds; NICE TA464 bisphosphonate recommendations), and explains that the goal is preventing the next, more serious fracture (especially hip/spine)

Gives honest, balanced BISPHOSPHONATE information: the benefit (substantial fracture-risk reduction) versus the side-effects she fears (osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femoral fracture are VERY RARE — MHRA Drug Safety Update July 2015 on the jaw and June 2011 on atypical femoral fractures; common issues are GI upset, manageable with correct administration) — putting the tiny absolute risks in proportion

Covers the full package: bloods before starting (bone profile including calcium, renal function and vitamin D; correct low calcium or vitamin D first), calcium and vitamin D (she takes little; NOGG 2024: calcium intake of at least 700 mg a day, ideally from diet), weight-bearing/resistance exercise, smoking/alcohol, falls prevention; dental check before/with bisphosphonates; correct oral administration (upright, empty stomach, water) — or alternatives (IV zoledronate, or denosumab per NICE TA204, which must not be stopped without a follow-on plan) if not tolerated/declined
Addresses the mother-fear (the engine): a treated osteoporosis is precisely how she AVOIDS her mother’s outcome; frames treatment + falls prevention as protecting independence
Responds to the anxiety and catastrophising first; corrects misinformation with warmth, not dismissal, and surfaces the "becoming my mother" fear
Shares the decision and respects autonomy: gives her the real numbers to choose with rather than steam-rollering or simply accepting refusal based on scare stories; offers alternatives

Safety-nets and follows up: how to take the medication and what side-effects genuinely warrant contact (jaw pain, thigh/groin pain, severe reflux), dental advice, calcium/vitD, a review of tolerance/adherence and a re-assessment plan (NOGG 2024: oral bisphosphonate for at least 5 years, then reassess fracture risk) — a shared, informed plan

worked.txt: "Let’s take the fear down a notch with the truth. ‘Thin bones’ — osteoporosis — means your bones are less dense than ideal, so they break more easily than they should. It does NOT mean they’re crumbling, and it does not mean a wheelchair. It means we have a clear, treatable risk we can act on now — which is far better than not knowing."

"Here’s why your case is one I do want to treat: the wrist you broke in the garden — that was a ‘fragility fracture’, a break from a minor fall that strong bone would have shrugged off. That fracture, plus the scan, plus your mum’s history, tells me your risk of a worse break — a hip or spine — is high enough that treating it really pays off. The whole aim is to stop the NEXT one."

"Now the jaw thing, because I’m not going to dodge it. The jaw problem you read about is real but genuinely rare — a tiny fraction of people, mostly after major dental surgery or at cancer doses, not the dose for bones. The thigh-bone one is rare too. Set against that: these tablets meaningfully cut your chance of a broken hip — the break that, frankly, is the one that steals independence. The maths is firmly on the side of treating."

"Can I gently ask — is your mum in your mind through all this? … Her hip, the home, losing her so soon after. That makes complete sense, and I’m so sorry. But here’s the thing to hold onto: treating your bones and preventing falls is EXACTLY how we keep you from going the way she did. This is your chance to not become that story."

"It’s not just a tablet either. Calcium and vitamin D, which you’re low on; weight-bearing and a bit of strength exercise, which genuinely builds bone; staying off the cigarettes. If you do take the tablet, a quick dental check first, take it upright with water on an empty stomach. And if you really don’t want the weekly tablet, there are other options — we have choices."

"So I’m not going to push something on you — I’m giving you the real numbers so YOU decide. My honest recommendation, with your fracture and your risk, is to treat. Take a day to think if you like. If you start the tablet and get bad heartburn, jaw pain, or thigh/groin pain, tell me. Let’s sort your calcium and vitamin D today either way, and I’ll review how you’re getting on. You came in terrified your bones are crumbling — they’re not, and we’ve got a real plan to keep you strong."

f.learning: A T-score ≤−2.5 is osteoporosis, and a low-trauma (fragility) fracture plus a high FRAX places this patient firmly in the treat category (NICE NG259 risk assessment; NOGG 2024 thresholds; NICE TA464) — the goal is preventing the next, more serious fracture (hip/spine). The first task is accurate reframing: osteoporosis is reduced bone density and increased fracture risk — treatable and modifiable — NOT "crumbling" or inevitable disability, the catastrophic picture night-time googling produces. The second is honest, balanced bisphosphonate information: the feared harms (osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical femoral fracture) are very rare and dose/context-dependent (MHRA Drug Safety Update, July 2015 and June 2011), while the fracture-prevention benefit is substantial; common GI effects are manageable with correct administration. Add the full package — calcium/vitamin D, weight-bearing/resistance exercise, smoking/alcohol, falls prevention, dental check — and offer alternatives if declined/not tolerated. The examinable hidden agenda is the mother who fractured a hip, went to a home and died within a year; treatment plus falls prevention is precisely how she AVOIDS that fate. Reframe with warmth, give real numbers, and support an informed, shared decision rather than steam-rollering or accepting a scare-story refusal.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG259 Osteoporosis: risk assessment (July 2026) · NICE TA464 (2017) · NICE TA204 (2010) · NOGG 2024 · MHRA Drug Safety Update (June 2011; July 2015) · BNF
knowledge.summary: A T-score of −2.7 after a low-trauma wrist fracture is osteoporosis with a fragility fracture: treat to prevent the next, more serious fracture. Reframe “crumbling” accurately, give honest proportionate information on the rare side effects, and let her make an informed choice.

points.t: A T-score of −2.5 or lower is osteoporosis; with a fragility fracture it is established osteoporosis. A fragility fracture is a break from a fall at standing height or less. It means higher fracture risk, not a skeleton that is crumbling or inevitable disability.

NICE NG259 Osteoporosis: risk assessment (July 2026): estimate the 10-year fracture risk (FRAX or QFracture). NICE TA464 bases bisphosphonate eligibility on the absolute fracture risk from that NICE assessment (CG146, now NG259). NOGG 2024: oral alendronate or risedronate, or IV zoledronate, are first-line; people at very high risk are referred for consideration of anabolic treatment.

Check for secondary causes and treatment safety: bone profile including calcium, renal function, and vitamin D, with other tests as indicated. Correct low calcium or vitamin D first. NOGG 2024: calcium intake of at least 700 mg a day, ideally from diet, with supplements if intake is low.

BNF: alendronic acid 70 mg once weekly, swallowed whole with a full glass of plain water on an empty stomach, at least 30 minutes before food or other medicines, staying upright for 30 minutes. Avoid in significant renal impairment (threshold per BNF).

points.h: The feared side effects, in proportion
points.t: MHRA Drug Safety Update (July 2015): the risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw in osteoporosis treatment is small compared with cancer doses; advise good oral hygiene, routine dental check-ups and reporting mouth problems. MHRA (June 2011): atypical femoral fractures are rare, mainly with long-term use — report thigh, hip or groin pain. Upper GI irritation is the common problem.

NOGG 2024: plan oral bisphosphonate for at least 5 years (IV for at least 3) and then reassess fracture risk. If oral treatment is declined or not tolerated: IV zoledronate, or denosumab (NICE TA204), which must not be stopped without a follow-on plan. NICE TA464 has a patient decision aid showing personal benefit and risk.

Osteoporosis with a fragility fracture, high fracture risk, low calcium intake — explained as fracture risk, not disability.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.

Idea (bones crumbling, tablets poison), concern (becoming her mother), expectation (to avoid the tablets).

When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.

model.text: Hello Mrs Naylor, I’m one of the GPs. You’re ringing about your bone scan — what have you been told so far, and how are you feeling about it?
model.why: Checks what she knows and how she feels first

model.text: That my bones are thin. I was up half the night reading. Does it mean they’re crumbling? That I’ll end up bent over, or in a wheelchair? And those bone tablets rot your jaw, don’t they? I don’t want them. Is there anything natural? I just want to know how bad it is.

That sounds like a frightening night. Let’s take it step by step: what the scan shows, what it means for you, and then the options, including your worries about the tablets. You’ll get straight answers. Is that alright?
model.why: Acknowledges distress and sets a clear agenda

model.text: Yes. Please.
Can I check a few things first? The wrist — how did it happen?
I tripped in the garden and put my hand out. Just a normal fall.
How is it now, and have you had any back pain, loss of height or other breaks?
model.why: Screens for vertebral fracture and other fractures

model.text: The wrist’s mending. No back trouble that I’ve noticed.
What do you eat and drink in a day — milk, cheese, yoghurt? And do you take any vitamin D?
model.why: Assesses calcium intake and vitamin D

model.text: Not much dairy, to be honest. No vitamins.
Any falls apart from the garden, problems with your balance, or trouble with your teeth or gums?
model.why: Falls risk and dental baseline before treatment

model.text: No, just that one fall. Teeth are fine as far as I know.
And any indigestion or problems swallowing?
model.why: Screens for upper GI problems relevant to oral bisphosphonates

model.text: No.
You said “bent over” and “wheelchair”. Is there a picture in your mind when you say that — someone you’ve seen?
model.why: Explores the image behind the catastrophising

model.text: (pause) My mum. She broke her hip, went into a nursing home, and she was gone within a year. I keep thinking that’s me.
I’m so sorry. That must have been awful to watch, and it explains why last night felt so frightening. Is that the real fear — becoming your mum?
model.why: Names the deeper fear with empathy

model.text: Yes. That’s it exactly.

Then let me be honest with you. Osteoporosis means your bones are less dense than they should be, so they break more easily. It doesn’t mean they’re crumbling, and it doesn’t mean a wheelchair. It means there’s a risk we can see and act on.

Your wrist was what we call a fragility fracture — a break from a fall that strong bone would have coped with. Together with your scan, your early menopause and your mum’s hip, your risk of a more serious break, like a hip, is high enough that treatment is well worth it. The whole aim is to stop the next one.
model.why: Explains why the fracture puts her in the treatment group

model.text: So treatment would stop me ending up like Mum?
It lowers that risk, together with keeping you strong and steady on your feet. That’s exactly how we avoid her story.
model.why: Links treatment to her concern without over-promising

model.text: Now the jaw. It’s a real side effect, but rare, and much rarer at bone-strength doses than at the high doses used for cancer. The thigh-bone fracture you may have read about is rare too, mainly after many years. The common problem is indigestion, and taking it the right way helps. I can go through a decision aid with you that shows, out of 100 women like you, how many fractures are prevented.
model.why: Balanced, proportionate risk information with a decision aid

model.text: I didn’t realise it was that rare. What about something natural?

Some natural things really help, alongside a tablet rather than instead of it: more calcium in your diet or a supplement, vitamin D, weight-bearing and strength exercise, and staying off cigarettes. On their own they won’t lower your risk enough after a fracture like yours.
model.why: Calcium, vitamin D, exercise and smoking in context

model.text: If you chose the tablet, it would be alendronate once a week: first thing, with a full glass of water, then stay upright for half an hour before breakfast. Keep up dental check-ups. If a weekly tablet doesn’t suit you, there’s a once-a-year drip or an injection. Before any of it, I’d like a blood test for calcium, kidneys and vitamin D.
Can I think about it for a few days?
Of course. It’s your decision, and I’d rather you chose with the facts than with last night’s reading. My recommendation is to treat. Shall I book the blood test and send you the decision aid?
model.why: Respects autonomy while giving a clear recommendation

model.text: Yes, please do.

If you do start, tell us about jaw or mouth pain, new thigh or groin pain, or heartburn or pain on swallowing. And any sudden back pain, or another fall, let us know. I’ll call you in a week with the bloods and your decision. What will you say to anyone who asks what the doctor said?
model.why: Specific warning symptoms, dated follow-up and teach-back

model.text: That my bones are thinner but not crumbling, there’s a tablet that cuts the risk, and the jaw thing is rare. And to eat more cheese.

social.t: Her mother’s hip fracture led to a nursing home and death within a year. This memory drives both the catastrophising and the reluctance to take treatment.
Night-time searching produced frightening but inaccurate pictures. Offer reliable sources and a decision aid rather than dismissing what she read.

legal.t: GMC Decision making and consent (2020): share the information she needs to decide, including the risks she cares about, and respect her choice. If she declines, record the discussion and offer to revisit it.

professional.t: Give a clear recommendation and personalised numbers (NICE TA464 patient decision aid), then let her decide. Neither steamroll nor accept a refusal based on misinformation.
A fragility fracture should prompt bone-health assessment; confirm the fracture liaison service or practice has a plan for treatment, adherence and reassessment.

community.t: Royal Osteoporosis Society helpline and leaflets; local strength-and-balance or exercise classes; NHS Smokefree support if needed; dentist for routine check-ups.

redFlags: New back pain or height loss — possible vertebral fracture
Dysphagia or active upper GI disease — caution with oral bisphosphonates
psychosocial: Her mother’s hip fracture, nursing home and death
Diet and calcium intake; health anxiety after online searching
ice: Idea: “My bones are crumbling and the tablets are poison.”
Concern: becoming her mother — a hip fracture, a care home, an early death
Expectation: to know how bad it is and to avoid the tablets

playbook.diagnosis: Postmenopausal osteoporosis (hip T-score −2.7) with a fragility wrist fracture and high FRAX risk; risk factors early menopause, maternal hip fracture and past smoking; low calcium intake.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your bones are less dense than they should be, so they break more easily — that’s what happened to your wrist. They’re not crumbling. It’s a risk we can measure and lower.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re frightened of ending up like your mum. Treating your bones and keeping you steady is exactly how we try to stop that happening.”
management.psychosocial: Replace the internet picture with accurate information and a decision aid; give her time to decide with the facts.
sharedPlan: Bloods first: bone profile with calcium, renal function, vitamin D and secondary-cause tests as indicated
Recommend alendronate once weekly with correct technique; alternatives IV zoledronate or denosumab
Calcium at least 700 mg a day, vitamin D, weight-bearing and strength exercise, dental check-ups, falls prevention
safetyNet: Report jaw or mouth pain, thigh or groin pain, heartburn or painful swallowing, new back pain
Call in a week with bloods and decision; review tolerance and reassess after 5 years of oral treatment

pitfalls.intro: This telephone station is about risk communication. Candidates fail by leaving the fear untouched, by dismissing the side effects she has read about, or by giving a plan she cannot follow.

items.fail: Not explaining what the T-score means, or saying “your bones are very thin”.
items.why: Unclear explanation feeds the catastrophising; “explanation not tailored to the patient”.
items.fix: Osteoporosis means bones break more easily than they should — a risk, not a crumbling skeleton.

items.fail: Treating the wrist as incidental and offering calcium only.
items.why: A fragility fracture with osteoporosis is a treatment indication; NOGG 2024 puts bisphosphonates first-line.
items.fix: Explain that the wrist is the reason to treat, and that the aim is to prevent the next fracture.

items.fail: Prescribing alendronate without bloods, technique or dental advice.
items.why: Hypocalcaemia, low vitamin D or renal impairment must be checked first; poor technique causes oesophageal harm.
items.fix: Bloods first, clear technique, dental check-ups, and named warning symptoms.

items.fail: Brushing off the jaw fear as internet nonsense.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s concerns”; she will decline treatment and stop listening.
items.fix: Acknowledge it is real, put it in proportion (MHRA), and offer the decision aid.

items.fail: Never finding out about her mother.
items.why: The hidden agenda drives both fear and refusal; the Relating domain depends on it.
items.fix: Ask what “bent over, in a wheelchair” brings to mind, then connect treatment to avoiding that outcome.

items.fail: Ending with “have a think and let us know”.
items.why: No follow-up plan means no decision; “poor follow-up arrangements”.
items.fix: Book the bloods, send the decision aid, and agree a call in a week.

Fracture mechanism, back pain or height loss, other fractures, falls, calcium and vitamin D, teeth, reflux or swallowing.
“Bent over, in a wheelchair” is her mother. Name the fear of becoming her before explaining anything.
Osteoporosis as fracture risk; why the wrist fracture matters; rare side effects in proportion; decision aid; calcium, vitamin D and exercise; alendronate technique; alternatives.
Warning symptoms, bloods, a call in a week with her decision, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Either tells her not to worry and offers only calcium, or insists on alendronate and dismisses the jaw fear; never explains what the T-score means; misses her mother; no follow-up.
wordPics.pass: Explains osteoporosis and the significance of the fragility fracture; gives accurate information that ONJ and atypical fractures are rare; covers calcium, vitamin D and exercise; explains administration; offers alternatives and follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: surfaces the fear of becoming her mother and uses it to frame treatment as protecting independence; offers the NICE TA464 decision aid for personal numbers; supports a genuine informed choice with a clear recommendation; checks bloods before starting; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Don’t believe what you read online — the jaw thing is nonsense.”
avoid.instead: “The jaw problem is real, but rare at bone doses, and here’s how we reduce the risk further.”
avoid.why: Dismissing a real side effect costs trust; honest proportion wins it.

avoid.dont: “Your bones are very thin, so you really must take this.”
avoid.instead: “Your bones break more easily than they should, and treatment lowers that risk. The choice is yours, and I’d recommend it.”
avoid.why: Fear and pressure worsen catastrophising and undermine an informed decision.

avoid.dont: “Calcium and vitamin D should do the trick.”
avoid.instead: “Calcium and vitamin D help, but after a fracture like yours they aren’t enough on their own.”
avoid.why: Offering only supplements under-treats a high-risk patient with a fragility fracture.

SCA_MODELS.text: Now the jaw. It’s a real side effect, but rare, and much rarer at bone-strength doses than at the high doses used for cancer. The thigh-bone fracture you may have read about is rare too, mainly after many years. The common problem is indigestion, and taking it the right way helps. I can go through a decision aid with you that shows, out of 100 women like you, how many fractures are prevented.
SCA_MODELS.why: Balanced, proportionate risk information with a decision aid

SCA_MODELS.text: I didn’t realise it was that rare. What about something natural?

Some natural things really help, alongside a tablet rather than instead of it: more calcium in your diet or a supplement, vitamin D, weight-bearing and strength exercise, and staying off cigarettes. On their own they won’t lower your risk enough after a fracture like yours.
SCA_MODELS.why: Calcium, vitamin D, exercise and smoking in context

SCA_MODELS.text: If you chose the tablet, it would be alendronate once a week: first thing, with a full glass of water, then stay upright for half an hour before breakfast. Keep up dental check-ups. If a weekly tablet doesn’t suit you, there’s a once-a-year drip or an injection. Before any of it, I’d like a blood test for calcium, kidneys and vitamin D.
Can I think about it for a few days?
Of course. It’s your decision, and I’d rather you chose with the facts than with last night’s reading. My recommendation is to treat. Shall I book the blood test and send you the decision aid?
SCA_MODELS.why: Respects autonomy while giving a clear recommendation

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes, please do.

If you do start, tell us about jaw or mouth pain, new thigh or groin pain, or heartburn or pain on swallowing. And any sudden back pain, or another fall, let us know. I’ll call you in a week with the bloods and your decision. What will you say to anyone who asks what the doctor said?
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific warning symptoms, dated follow-up and teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: That my bones are thinner but not crumbling, there’s a tablet that cuts the risk, and the jaw thing is rare. And to eat more cheese.

SCA_STEM.name: Patricia Naylor
pmh: Wrist fracture 8 weeks ago after tripping in the garden
SCA_STEM.recent: DXA scan: hip T-score −2.7. FRAX: high risk. Family history: mother had a hip fracture.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephone appointment to discuss her bone scan result.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG259 Osteoporosis: risk assessment (July 2026) · NICE TA464 (2017) · NICE TA204 (2010) · NOGG 2024 · MHRA Drug Safety Update (June 2011; July 2015) · BNF
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A T-score of −2.7 after a low-trauma wrist fracture is osteoporosis with a fragility fracture: treat to prevent the next, more serious fracture. Reframe “crumbling” accurately, give honest proportionate information on the rare side effects, and let her make an informed choice.

points.t: A T-score of −2.5 or lower is osteoporosis; with a fragility fracture it is established osteoporosis. A fragility fracture is a break from a fall at standing height or less. It means higher fracture risk, not a skeleton that is crumbling or inevitable disability.

NICE NG259 Osteoporosis: risk assessment (July 2026): estimate the 10-year fracture risk (FRAX or QFracture). NICE TA464 bases bisphosphonate eligibility on the absolute fracture risk from that NICE assessment (CG146, now NG259). NOGG 2024: oral alendronate or risedronate, or IV zoledronate, are first-line; people at very high risk are referred for consideration of anabolic treatment.

Check for secondary causes and treatment safety: bone profile including calcium, renal function, and vitamin D, with other tests as indicated. Correct low calcium or vitamin D first. NOGG 2024: calcium intake of at least 700 mg a day, ideally from diet, with supplements if intake is low.

BNF: alendronic acid 70 mg once weekly, swallowed whole with a full glass of plain water on an empty stomach, at least 30 minutes before food or other medicines, staying upright for 30 minutes. Avoid in significant renal impairment (threshold per BNF).

points.h: The feared side effects, in proportion
points.t: MHRA Drug Safety Update (July 2015): the risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw in osteoporosis treatment is small compared with cancer doses; advise good oral hygiene, routine dental check-ups and reporting mouth problems. MHRA (June 2011): atypical femoral fractures are rare, mainly with long-term use — report thigh, hip or groin pain. Upper GI irritation is the common problem.

NOGG 2024: plan oral bisphosphonate for at least 5 years (IV for at least 3) and then reassess fracture risk. If oral treatment is declined or not tolerated: IV zoledronate, or denosumab (NICE TA204), which must not be stopped without a follow-on plan. NICE TA464 has a patient decision aid showing personal benefit and risk.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Checked what she understood and how she felt before explaining; let her voice the fear of the tablets.
Diet, calcium intake, smoking history, activity and independence; what her mother’s decline means to her.
Picked up “bent over, wheelchair” and explored the picture behind it; heard “something natural” as a wish for permission to decline.
Idea (bones crumbling, tablets poison), concern (becoming her mother), expectation (to avoid the tablets).
Bone profile with calcium, renal function, vitamin D and other secondary-cause tests as indicated; dental status; FRAX already done.
Primary postmenopausal osteoporosis vs secondary causes; asked about vertebral symptoms and further fractures.
Screened for back pain or height loss (vertebral fracture), dysphagia or reflux, and falls; renal function before alendronate.
Osteoporosis with a fragility fracture, high fracture risk, low calcium intake — explained as fracture risk, not disability.
Oral bisphosphonate recommended with correct administration; calcium and vitamin D; exercise; alternatives offered; informed choice with the NICE TA464 decision aid.
Falls prevention, smoking status, dental care; upper GI tolerability considered.
Named warning symptoms; bloods and decision call in a week; review of tolerance and reassessment after 5 years of oral treatment.

social.t: Her mother’s hip fracture led to a nursing home and death within a year. This memory drives both the catastrophising and the reluctance to take treatment.
Night-time searching produced frightening but inaccurate pictures. Offer reliable sources and a decision aid rather than dismissing what she read.

legal.t: GMC Decision making and consent (2020): share the information she needs to decide, including the risks she cares about, and respect her choice. If she declines, record the discussion and offer to revisit it.

professional.t: Give a clear recommendation and personalised numbers (NICE TA464 patient decision aid), then let her decide. Neither steamroll nor accept a refusal based on misinformation.
A fragility fracture should prompt bone-health assessment; confirm the fracture liaison service or practice has a plan for treatment, adherence and reassessment.

community.t: Royal Osteoporosis Society helpline and leaflets; local strength-and-balance or exercise classes; NHS Smokefree support if needed; dentist for routine check-ups.

redFlags: New back pain or height loss — possible vertebral fracture
Dysphagia or active upper GI disease — caution with oral bisphosphonates
psychosocial: Her mother’s hip fracture, nursing home and death
Diet and calcium intake; health anxiety after online searching
ice: Idea: “My bones are crumbling and the tablets are poison.”
Concern: becoming her mother — a hip fracture, a care home, an early death
Expectation: to know how bad it is and to avoid the tablets

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Postmenopausal osteoporosis (hip T-score −2.7) with a fragility wrist fracture and high FRAX risk; risk factors early menopause, maternal hip fracture and past smoking; low calcium intake.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your bones are less dense than they should be, so they break more easily — that’s what happened to your wrist. They’re not crumbling. It’s a risk we can measure and lower.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re frightened of ending up like your mum. Treating your bones and keeping you steady is exactly how we try to stop that happening.”
management.psychosocial: Replace the internet picture with accurate information and a decision aid; give her time to decide with the facts.
sharedPlan: Bloods first: bone profile with calcium, renal function, vitamin D and secondary-cause tests as indicated
Recommend alendronate once weekly with correct technique; alternatives IV zoledronate or denosumab
Calcium at least 700 mg a day, vitamin D, weight-bearing and strength exercise, dental check-ups, falls prevention
safetyNet: Report jaw or mouth pain, thigh or groin pain, heartburn or painful swallowing, new back pain
Call in a week with bloods and decision; review tolerance and reassess after 5 years of oral treatment

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This telephone station is about risk communication. Candidates fail by leaving the fear untouched, by dismissing the side effects she has read about, or by giving a plan she cannot follow.

items.fail: Not explaining what the T-score means, or saying “your bones are very thin”.
items.why: Unclear explanation feeds the catastrophising; “explanation not tailored to the patient”.
items.fix: Osteoporosis means bones break more easily than they should — a risk, not a crumbling skeleton.

items.fail: Treating the wrist as incidental and offering calcium only.
items.why: A fragility fracture with osteoporosis is a treatment indication; NOGG 2024 puts bisphosphonates first-line.
items.fix: Explain that the wrist is the reason to treat, and that the aim is to prevent the next fracture.

items.fail: Prescribing alendronate without bloods, technique or dental advice.
items.why: Hypocalcaemia, low vitamin D or renal impairment must be checked first; poor technique causes oesophageal harm.
items.fix: Bloods first, clear technique, dental check-ups, and named warning symptoms.

items.fail: Brushing off the jaw fear as internet nonsense.
items.why: “Does not respond to the patient’s concerns”; she will decline treatment and stop listening.
items.fix: Acknowledge it is real, put it in proportion (MHRA), and offer the decision aid.

items.fail: Never finding out about her mother.
items.why: The hidden agenda drives both fear and refusal; the Relating domain depends on it.
items.fix: Ask what “bent over, in a wheelchair” brings to mind, then connect treatment to avoiding that outcome.

items.fail: Ending with “have a think and let us know”.
items.why: No follow-up plan means no decision; “poor follow-up arrangements”.
items.fix: Book the bloods, send the decision aid, and agree a call in a week.
